newsitem.title: UK: UK's AIM market looks for growth on 2nd birthday.
newsitem.headline: UK's AIM market looks for growth on 2nd birthday.

text.p: Two years to the day after the formation of London's Alternative Investment Market (AIM), market watchers speaking at a conference on Thursday reflected on the obstacles preventing the small-companies exchange achieving a wider appeal to investors.

AIM, set up by the London Stock Exchange as a vehicle for smaller, fast-growing companies not yet mature enough to join the main market, has claimed the market as a huge success, pointing to the 284 companies it now includes.

"It's been a major success and a major achievement of the London Stock Exchange," said Graham Cole, director of Corporate Finance at brokerage Beeson Gregory, at today's London Alternative Investment Market conference.
"The odd disaster should not divert us."
Theresa Wallis, the market's chief executive, said listing on the market had given companies greater confidence and a higher public profile.
AIM's 284 companies have raised a total of 1.3 billion stg through their listings and have a current market value of just under six billion stg.

Yet a sharp gain in the AIM index in the first two months of the year failed to hold and the index has slipped back since the end of February. By Friday's close it was up just 1.6 percent since the end of 1996.
It is a performance that has fallen short of some expectations. As a proportion of the market as a whole, AIM companies made up just 0.5 percent of the total value of quoted British companies.
Fund managers and brokers speaking at the conference saw the lack of news on companies' activities as a reason for low liquidity levels.
"Communication is important," said Andrew Buchanan, a fund manager specialising in AIM stocks at Rutherford Fund Managers. "Institutions need a better understanding of the individual businesses."
Conference delegates said a prevalence of stocks with low free market capital -- shares not owned by company directors -- also discouraged investment in AIM companies.
However, others said patience was required when dealing on AIM.
"OK, a profit is not a profit unless you can get it, but you have to work at it on AIM," said Robert Mitchell, a fund manager at Ivory & Sime Baronsmead Plc.

Investment managers said companies that were undercapitalised at the time of flotation were off-putting. They said such companies would not have the finance to achieve their potential growth and would be forced to seek further funds.
Adair Turner, director-general of the Confederation of British Industry, said the level of communication between the investment community and small businesses was needed for AIM to grow further.
"There is not a finance gap, there is an information gap," said Turner. "Investors need to talk to people with good business ideas."
AIM's launch in June 1995 by the London Stock Exchange has been followed by the creation of junior equity markets in other European centres.
But AIM's equivalents in Paris, Frankfurt, Brussels and Amsterdam have so far attracted only a handful of entrants.

One issue that has dogged the market in its first two years is the key role of brokerages who take the tightly-defined role of "nominated adviser" to companies joining the market -- effectively a guarantor of their financial stability.
Yet the rules defining the role of the so-called "Nomads" were tightened last month and speakers at the conference said awareness of their role had increased.
Beeson Gregory said it had turned down 140 companies which had applied for a listing.
